falas.txt: This is Nvidia. Thirty three years of work, with one man at the top.

v.k: Thirty three years. *One CEO*.

falas.txt: On November twelfth, twenty twenty six, he resigned.

v.k: November 12, 2026: *he resigned*.

falas.txt: And the tower didn't move.

v.k: The tower *didn't move*.

falas.txt: Five days later, Nvidia reported its biggest quarter ever.

v.sub: Revenue in a single quarter. Up 103% in a year.

falas.txt: A hundred and fifteen point eight billion dollars in three months. Double the year before.
Its customers didn't leave. Because they can't.

v.sub: The customers didn't leave. They can't.

falas.txt: Think about how strange that is. Rivals have built faster chips for some jobs.
They've built cheaper chips.
They have billions of dollars, and some of the best engineers alive.
And they still can't pull Nvidia's customers away.
Because the thing holding those customers isn't the chip.

v.k: What holds them *isn't the chip*.

falas.txt: So what is it?
There are five locks.

nomes: A way to talk to the chip
Chips, network and software as one

falas.txt: Four of them are software and hardware.
The fifth is something almost no company is willing to do.
And it's the one that left the building on November twelfth.

v.k: It may have *left the building* on November 12.

falas.txt: Lock one. The language.
Twenty years ago, a graphics chip did one thing. It drew video games.

tit: A graphics chip only spoke *one language*.

falas.txt: It was incredibly good at doing thousands of small calculations at the same time.
Scientists wanted that power. But to use it, they had to disguise their math as a picture, and trick the chip into drawing it.
In two thousand six, Nvidia announced a way out. It's called CUDA.

tit: 2006: *CUDA*. Talk to the chip in normal code.

falas.txt: With CUDA, you write ordinary code, and the chip runs it on thousands of cores at once.
And Nvidia gave it away for free.

v.k: And it was *free*.

falas.txt: Free sounds generous. It's also the lock.
Because CUDA only runs on Nvidia chips.

v.l2: It only runs on Nvidia chips.

falas.txt: Every line of code written in it, is a line that can't simply move to anyone else.

v.k: Every line written is a line that *can't simply move*.

falas.txt: Lock two. The libraries.
Almost nobody writes CUDA directly anymore.

tit: Nobody starts from zero. *They start here*.

falas.txt: They use libraries. Finished, tested pieces of software that sit on top of it.
One for neural networks. One for weather. One for chemistry. One for video.
Nvidia's own filings count hundreds of them.
Each one took years to write. And years more to make fast.

v.k: Years to write. *Years more* to make fast.

falas.txt: And on top of those sit the tools the whole AI world builds with.
Then the models. Then the apps you actually use.
So when a rival ships a new chip, it isn't competing with a chip.

lb: Most tools: work out of the box

falas.txt: It's competing with twenty years of software that already works.
The new tools usually run on Nvidia first. Everyone else gets support later, if they get it at all.
A faster chip that can't run your code, isn't faster. It's a paperweight.

v.k: A faster chip that can't run your code is *a paperweight*.

falas.txt: Lock three. The habit.
In twenty twelve, three researchers in Toronto entered a contest to recognize objects in photos.

v.sub: Three researchers enter an image recognition contest.

falas.txt: They trained their program on two Nvidia gaming cards. The kind you could buy in a store.
The code was about six thousand lines of CUDA.
It crushed everything else in the contest. It's called AlexNet, and it started the modern AI boom.

v.k: Its name: *AlexNet*. It started the AI boom.

falas.txt: And from that day on, if you wanted to do AI research, you did it the way they did.

v.k: From then on, everyone did it *their way*.

falas.txt: Today, Nvidia says more than seven and a half million developers use CUDA and its tools.

r1: DEVELOPERS USING CUDA AND NVIDIA TOOLS

falas.txt: That's seven and a half million people who learned on it at university,

v.k: They *learned* on it.

falas.txt: got hired because they knew it,

v.k: They got *hired* for it.

falas.txt: and wrote years of working code in it.

v.k: They wrote *years of code* in it.

falas.txt: To switch chips, a company doesn't just buy new hardware. It has to retrain its people, and rewrite and re-test what they built.

v.k: Switching means *retraining people* and *rewriting code*.

falas.txt: Quick question, before the next lock.
If you ran an AI company, how much cheaper would a rival chip have to be, before you'd rewrite everything? Twenty percent? Fifty?
Put your number in the comments. Then see if lock four changes it.
Lock four. The whole machine.
A modern AI model isn't trained on one chip. It's trained on thousands of them, acting as one.

tit: One chip is useless. *Thousands, acting as one*.

falas.txt: Which means the connections between the chips matter as much as the chips.
In twenty twenty, Nvidia bought a networking company called Mellanox, for about seven billion dollars.

v.k: 2020: Nvidia buys Mellanox for about *$7 billion*.

falas.txt: At the time, it looked like a side business.

v.k: It looked like *a side business*.

falas.txt: Now Nvidia doesn't sell you a chip. It sells you the chips, the network between them, and the software on top. Designed together, delivered as one rack.
And it replaces that whole machine with a new generation about once a year.

v.k: A new generation *about once a year*.

falas.txt: By the time a rival matches one, the next one is already shipping.

v.k: Match one, and *the next is already shipping*.

falas.txt: In fiscal twenty twenty six, Nvidia's data center business brought in a hundred and ninety four billion dollars.
And its data center networking revenue grew a hundred and forty two percent in a single year.
So a rival doesn't have to beat one product. It has to beat three, that were built to fit each other.

v.k: Not one product. *Three*, built to fit each other.

falas.txt: That's four locks.

nomes: A way to talk to the chip
Chips, network and software as one

falas.txt: A language only their chips speak.
Twenty years of libraries.
Seven and a half million trained people.
And a whole machine, sold as one.
All four can be copied. With enough money, and enough engineers.

v.k: Money. Engineers. Time.

falas.txt: A-M-D is trying. Intel is trying. Google builds its own chips, with its own software.

v.k: AMD, Intel and Google are all trying.

falas.txt: The fifth lock is why it's taking them so long.

nomes: A way to talk to the chip
Chips, network and software as one

falas.txt: And it has nothing to do with engineering.

v.k: It has *nothing to do* with engineering.

falas.txt: Lock five.

fonte: THE NEW YORKER (2023), VIA SECONDARY REPORTS

falas.txt: Go back to two thousand six. Nvidia is a company that sells graphics cards to gamers.
And its C-E-O decides to put CUDA on every single chip. Including the ones for people who will never use it.

v.k: CUDA went on *every* chip. Even for people who never used it.

falas.txt: That made every chip more expensive to design. And for years, almost nobody wanted it.

v.k: More cost. For years, *almost no demand*.

falas.txt: Investors hated it. By the end of two thousand eight, Nvidia's stock had reportedly fallen about seventy percent.
Nvidia kept paying for it anyway. Through two thousand nine. Ten. Eleven.

v.k: Nvidia *kept paying* anyway.

falas.txt: Then AlexNet happened.
And by one account, it still took until around twenty sixteen for Wall Street to believe it.
Ten years, of paying for something the market didn't want.

vao: OF PAYING FOR SOMETHING THE MARKET DID NOT WANT

falas.txt: That's lock five. The lost decade.
Any big company can afford the engineers.

v.sub: Any big company can afford the engineers.

falas.txt: Almost none can afford to look wrong for ten years in a row.

v.sub: Almost none can afford to look wrong for ten years.

falas.txt: And it's worse for a rival today than it was for Nvidia then.

la: Must fund software for a decade
While answering to investors every quarter
lb: Adds to it every single day

falas.txt: A rival has to fund ten years of software.
Against a twenty year head start.
While the company it's chasing earns more than a hundred billion dollars a quarter, and spends part of it widening the gap.
The only ones seriously trying are the ones rich enough to build chips for themselves. Google. Amazon. Microsoft.

v.k: The ones trying: companies *rich enough to wait*.

falas.txt: They're not copying Nvidia to sell against it. They're copying it to stop paying it.

v.k: Not to sell against Nvidia. To *stop paying* it.

falas.txt: Is this lock perfect? No. And you should know where the cracks are.
Training a brand new model is where CUDA is strongest.
But running a finished model, millions of times a day, is simpler work. It's easier to move to another chip.
And that's exactly where the custom chips are aimed.

v.leg: THIS IS WHERE THE CUSTOM CHIPS ARE AIMED

falas.txt: So the lock isn't that nobody can ever leave. It's that leaving costs years. And almost nobody has years to spare.

v.k: Leaving costs years. Almost nobody has *years to spare*.

falas.txt: So here's what a real copy would need.

v.cab: WHAT A REAL COPY WOULD NEED

falas.txt: A language people actually use.
Twenty years of libraries.
Millions of trained developers.
And a leader willing to look wrong for a decade.
You can copy a chip in three years.

v.l1: You can copy a chip in three years.

falas.txt: You can't copy a decade nobody wanted to pay for.

v.l2: You can't copy a decade nobody wanted.

falas.txt: If you know someone who thinks Nvidia is finished because its founder is gone, send them this video.
Because there's one thing they'd be right about.

v.s: The one thing they'd be right about

falas.txt: Go back to the tower.
The founder is gone. The chips, the network, the software and the developers are all still there.
Nvidia's board says the roadmap continues without interruption. And for now, the numbers agree.

v.k: The board: the roadmap continues *without interruption*.

falas.txt: The four locks don't need him.

v.k: Four locks *don't need him*.

falas.txt: But the fifth one did.
CUDA exists because one person was allowed to be wrong for ten years.

v.sub: CUDA exists because one person could be wrong for ten years.

falas.txt: A founder can do that. An interim C-E-O, with a board and a search committee, almost never can.

v.sub: A founder can do that. A caretaker almost never can.

falas.txt: So that's the real reason nobody can copy Nvidia.
Nobody can copy the last twenty years.

v.l1: Nobody can copy the last twenty years.

falas.txt: The real question is who, inside Nvidia, gets to start the next ten.

v.l2: Who gets to start the next ten?

falas.txt: The software is one link in a chain. And almost every link has a company like this hiding in it.
